title: The Lowe Post Is Back—and It’s a Newsletter Now
subtitle: Why I’m writing again, and why I’d love for you to join me
contentHtml:
These are the first formal words I’ve written in two years—since the morning I was ironing my suit for television at a hotel in Los Angeles, where I had arrived from New York only 30 hours prior, when an ESPN executive called and read a 30-second script informing me that my almost 15 years of work there were over, effective that second. (The news broke about two minutes later.)

As a teenager, I had dreamed of being a sportswriter; basketball and baseball were my favorites. My path to becoming a Basketball Guy on national television was unlikely, to put it mildly. I chickened out on journalism in college; rediscovered it after forays into teaching and academia; cut my teeth as a criminal justice reporter at a newspaper; and shoved my way into NBA writing starting around 2009 because that was the sport every editor told me they needed help covering.

Subscribe now

If you had told me in 2011, when Bill Simmons hired me to work at Grantland (and, by extension, ESPN), that I would be anything other than a writer, I wouldn’t have really even understood what you were suggesting. The idea of being on television was beyond preposterous—not even a germ of an idea in any recess of my brain. Podcasts barely existed; I had never thought of myself as someone who could host anything.

The only reason I even have a podcast is that Bill and especially David Jacoby forced me to start one against my will. They said it would work, that I was ready. I protested that I was a writer first and only—that any distraction from writing would dilute the only thing of value I provided.

By the end of my time at ESPN, my podcast—The Lowe Post—somehow seemed the most important element of my job. I was a small cog in the TV machine. Writing still mattered to some folks on the dot-com side, but it was beginning to feel more like a space-filling obligation.

When I was approached on the street or at games, it was almost always about my podcast. It gave readers a glimpse into my personality—and those of my guests—without sacrificing too much analytical rigor. It was loose. It allowed for tangents. (It even became the crow bar to reopen the emotional crevices once and now again filled by New York’s National League baseball club.)

Wherever I landed next, I knew the podcast would be the main thing. When I joined The Ringer/Spotify, we discussed building a newsletter to supplement my revived podcast. I tabled it for a year. I wanted to understand the rhythm of my new job, but I also wanted to see if I missed writing.

My life would be easier without it. I’d have more time for … everything: driving car pools, hanging with my wife and our friends, reading books—even fiction!—and spending time with my daughter. She is 11, which means there is only so much time until friends outrank Daddy. (When no one is watching, she still loves to snuggle. She loves the Mets now, too; she has built her own physical “Mets Corner” of jerseys and memorabilia in her bedroom.)

Six months ago, I was fine being done with writing even though “writer” was once core to my identity. I was busy enough with my podcast, occasional appearances on Bill’s, some TV work for Amazon Prime, travel, watching games, and reporting.

Almost against my will, that began to change. Now and then, someone would ask if I might write again. Not everyone listens to podcasts; they don’t have hour-long commutes, or they prefer music during workouts. They wanted something to read for 10 minutes over lunch (or on the toilet).

And I began to feel as if my brain were operating at 90 percent capacity—that it had sloughed away one tool that helped all the other tools work better.

I read a recent op-ed in The New York Times in which Joe Cruz, a professor at Williams College, wondered whether perhaps the intellectual community at large had fetishized the importance of writing. Cruz argued (and I’m paraphrasing) that oral examinations require a higher level of thinking—that only students who had truly mastered the material could muster the improvisational mental dexterity to go toe-to-toe on the fly.

There is something to that. My brain crackles when Bill pivots suddenly into a debate about some big-picture basketball issue or 1970s NBA lore.

But writing ignites other parts of your thought process that might go dormant without it: word choice, language, sentence structure, the underpinnings of communication. Putting words on paper—the permanence of it—forces you to take an extra beat and make sure your material holds up: Does this trade really make sense? Would this rule change actually work, or does it have bad ripple effects? You game out your own ideas. You interrogate them. That process takes you to new places, notions you hadn’t contemplated.

Those two methods of communication—and the thought processes that undergird them—are complementary. Honing one hones the other. The preparation inherent in writing can nourish your in-the-moment verbal flexibility, and perhaps vice versa.

Reading also has to keep mattering as technology shatters attention spans and rewires our brains in ways we never imagined or really asked for. If humans stop reading and writing, parts of our brains will wither.

This is not intended as grandstanding. A lot of this is selfish: Writing will make me better at other parts of my job. I also want my voice—my true writing voice—to be out in the world as larger forces inexorably homogenize the way things look and sound.

The use of AI to create bogus art—poems, essays, music—is, frankly, gross. Part of being a human is the struggle to create, to articulate—to try to express something authentic, to fail, to try again.

I recently dropped my daughter off at a birthday party where the parents boasted about asking ChatGPT for advice on what color balloons to use. I hear more and more about relying on AI to set vacation itineraries. Have we really gotten this lazy? Do people no longer derive satisfaction from researching hotels, restaurants, excursions, color schemes? Using your brain that way is definitional to, like, being a living person.

During my hiatus from writing, I watched as my wife dove into the world of creative nonfiction—in her second language, no less—publishing essays, winning contests, and getting selected for prestigious week-long residencies. Seeing her revel in the struggle, and produce meaningful work, ignited something in me.

And so with some trepidation, I am reactivating this part of my brain—in hopes of finding old readers and new. This space will be different from the mammoth columns I wrote at ESPN. The baseline goal is one post a week, and the hope is to be brisker.

I try to be a jack-of-all-NBA-trades. I break down X’s and O’s, thanks in large part to sources all over basketball who have helped me hone my knowledge over the last 15 years. I hear tidbits that inform how I talk about teams, players, and transactions on my podcast; some of that reporting will infiltrate this space. I’m decent with the salary cap and fake trades. I’m a sucker for all the accoutrements around the game—art, courts, jerseys, announcers. I love digging into long-term trends, both in on-court strategy and rule changes, and in the business side of the NBA. Hopefully this space will have something for everyone.

This Substack will complement The Zach Lowe Show, so that they merge into one larger content hub. If we do a podcast segment on, say, a Knicks-Sixers series, I might follow up here with a more detailed analysis on some X’s-and-O’s nuance we glided over on the show because nitty-gritty breakdowns don’t work as well in audio form. The video clips and still images you might remember from my old columns could be part of that.

If I record my first podcast of the week on a Monday morning and there is a marquee matchup that night—Thunder-Spurs anyone?—then I might write a missive about that game, since it would be old-ish news by the time of my next episode. If I get wind of a newsy nugget and verify it, a quickie post on that could pop up in your inbox. If some minor but weirdly fascinating trade gets short shrift on the podcast, it might take center stage here.

I want this to be fun, not burdensome—for me and for you. There was a time I deeply enjoyed writing, even the head-pounding frustration and solitude of it. I want to see if I can find that again. I mean, this is basketball, right? It’s sports! It should be a hoot. I have to at least try; let’s maybe try together?

So … WELCOME (back) TO … The Lowe Post!
